author: eps
cardQuote: Thermostat managed through a hosted web service? I'm sorry but this is idiotic.
quote: Thermostat managed through a hosted web service? I'm sorry but this is idiotic. Looks neat though.
outcome: Google acquired Nest for $3.2B in 2014; the cloud thermostat became a mainstream model.
outcomeDetail: Nest shipped the thermostat, built a line of smart-home products, and was bought by Google for $3.2 billion in January 2014. The hosted-service approach the comment called idiotic became standard for connected devices.
note: The critic was right that a cloud-tied thermostat adds a dependency, but wrong that it was idiotic: remote control and learning became the product's selling points.

author: aliston
cardQuote: I'm not sure their brand is enough to allow them to compete.
quote:
When Warby Parker was first getting off the ground, the idea of buying glasses online was completely new. They've done a great job of validating the model, but now they're facing a lot of competition and I'm not sure their brand is enough to allow them to compete.

I ended up buying my two pairs of glasses from a competitor... The first pair was only $30, and that was only because I opted for a higher end lens. The second pair was a designer brand that was at a similar price point. Since the lens cost has gone down dramatically for all of the online retailers, on what basis is Warby Parker going to compete?

Glasses are an industry that is all about brand labels. For people that care about that sort of thing, they'll go buy RayBan or Gucci or whatever else over a Warby frame at a roughly similar price point. For folks that don't care about that sort of thing, they'll buy a cheaper non-name brand fram for less than the Warby price point.
storyTitle: Warby Parker Grabs New Investment, Closing $41.5M Round
outcome: Direct-listed in 2021; 300+ stores and about $872M revenue by 2025.
outcomeDetail: Warby Parker went public through a direct listing in September 2021 and kept opening stores, reaching 323 locations and $871.9 million in revenue by 2025. Its brand proved durable even as online eyewear competition increased.
note: The comment saw the coming competition but underestimated the brand and retail flywheel; Warby Parker became the category leader it doubted.

author: pbreit
cardQuote: I don't see Harry's having a credible story for being a premier blade manufacturer for a long time, if ever.
quote: Well, most tech companies go in the opposite direction: figuring out where they can add value and focusing on that. For Harry's that is/was design and marketing. I don't see Harry's having a credible story for being a premier blade manufacturer for a long time, if ever. And even then, their blades won't likely be any better than Gillette or Dorco. Still scratching my head on this one.
storyTitle: Razor Startup Harry’s Raises $75M, Pushing It Over $200M
outcome: Bought its German blade factory in 2014; valued at $1.7B in 2021 after Edgewell's $1.37B deal was blocked.
outcomeDetail: Harry's used the $75 million round discussed here to help buy the Feintechnik razor factory in Germany for $100 million in January 2014. Edgewell later agreed to buy Harry's for $1.37 billion, the FTC blocked the deal, and Harry's raised at a $1.7 billion valuation in 2021.
note: The comment doubted Harry's could become a real blade manufacturer; it had already bought a 94-year-old German factory, and the brand kept scaling.

author: roel_v
cardQuote: Key to subscription based businesses are retention and cost of customer acquisition.
quote: Key to subscription based businesses are retention and cost of customer acquisition. Which, I predict for this business with no knowledge about the industry at all, are low and high, respectively.
storyTitle: Dollar Shave Club Is Valued at $615M
outcome: Unilever bought Dollar Shave Club for $1B in 2016.
outcomeDetail: Unilever acquired Dollar Shave Club in July 2016 for a reported $1 billion in cash, about a year after this comment. The subscription razor startup became the reference exit for direct-to-consumer brands.
note: The comment predicted weak retention and expensive acquisition; the $1 billion exit showed the model could scale, even if the category later cooled.

author: hristov
cardQuote: The start-up graveyards are full of companies that have promised a mesh wireless system and have failed miserably.
quote:
No need to be baffled. The start-up graveyards are full of companies that have promised a mesh wireless system and have failed miserably. It is not fear of the unknown, it is a very healthy skepticism towards unsubstantiated marketing claims. Or, in other words -- it is fear of the vaporware.

If it all works as advertised, this would be great. But there is no reason to believe these ambitious marketing claims before there is actual product on the shelves.
storyTitle: Eero – Blanket your home in fast, reliable WiFi
outcome: Amazon acquired Eero for $97M in 2019; mesh Wi-Fi became a mainstream category.
outcomeDetail: Eero shipped its mesh routers, and Amazon bought the company for $97 million in 2019. Mesh systems became the default way to cover a home with Wi-Fi, and Eero remained a leading brand under Amazon.
note: The comment was right that mesh Wi-Fi had produced vaporware, but wrong to put Eero in that pile; it shipped and helped define the category.

author: ricw
cardQuote: And having written my PhD thesis on these things I know its a complete and utter pain. Chances for success: less than 1%.
quote:
I don't think these guys know how complex and difficult this is going to be. They might have an SDK out this year, but chances are its pretty rubbish. Its not as if others haven't tried. And having written my PhD thesis on these things I know its a complete and utter pain. 
Chances for success: less than 1%.
outcome: Samsung acquired SmartThings in 2014 in a deal estimated at up to $200M.
outcomeDetail: SmartThings shipped its hub and sensors and built a developer platform. Samsung bought the company in August 2014, with trade press estimating the price as high as $200 million, and it became the base of Samsung's smart-home strategy.
note: The 'less than 1%' forecast was wrong within two years; SmartThings became one of the first consumer IoT startups to score a major acquisition.

author: free2rhyme214
cardQuote: To me Fitbit is a feature that will be free and ubiquitous in the future.
quote:
To me Fitbit is a feature that will be free and ubiquitous in the future.

Just wait until developers have more time with Android Wear.
outcome: IPO'd in 2015; Google bought Fitbit for $2.1B in 2019.
outcomeDetail: Fitbit went public in June 2015 and remained the fifth-largest wearable maker by shipments in 2019. Google agreed to buy it for $2.1 billion, and the deal closed in 2021.
note: The 'feature that will be free' prediction missed the brand, distribution, and data assets that made Fitbit worth $2.1 billion to Google.

author: BurritoAlPastor
cardQuote: Acquired by who? It's a luxury niche brand.
quote:
Acquired by who? It's a luxury niche brand. Acquisition by one of the giants they integrate with (Apple, Amazon, Spotify, etc) would inevitably result in vendor lock-in (Apple buys them and now Amazon Music doesn't work anymore), which would be devastating to their reputation and customer sat. A "neutral" giant (LG?) could pick them up, but why? Who wants to diversify into luxury home stereo? That leaves major audio companies (Sennheiser? Bose?), but those are mostly already luxury brands, and cobranding ("Sonos by Sennheiser") could get complicated.

The nature of the market Sonos is working in means that whatever P/M fit they have is potentially compromised by being acquired. Weird, but that's luxury goods for ya.
storyTitle: What cracking open a Sonos One tells us about the Sonos IPO
outcome: IPO'd in 2018; still independent with about $1.44B in revenue in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Sonos completed its IPO in August 2018 and stayed independent, expanding from multi-room speakers into soundbars and headphones. Revenue was about $1.44 billion in 2025.
note: The comment dismissed Sonos as a 'luxury niche brand' with no plausible exit; it went public weeks later and remained a standalone public company.

author: jbob2000
cardQuote: This is ridiculous, these bikes are a fad.
quote:
This is ridiculous, these bikes are a fad. The company will get sold to a gym or furniture giant for pennies once people get bored and realize they paid $2,000 for a clothes hanger.

I will say it's an interesting take on an old business. Furniture and exercise equipment manufacturers have this problem where everybody buys their stuff and they go bankrupt because nobody needs new equipment after the initial purchase. So attaching the subscription business model to this might give them a bit more longevity!
storyTitle: Peloton raises $550M at a valuation of $4B
outcome: IPO'd in 2019 at $8.1B; peaked at $50B in 2021, then fell to about $1.3B by 2024.
outcomeDetail: Peloton went public in September 2019 at an $8.1 billion valuation and became a pandemic-era category leader. Its market value reached $50 billion in January 2021, then collapsed to about $1.3 billion by June 2024 as demand fell and losses mounted.
note: The 'sold for pennies' prediction was wrong: Peloton IPO'd and briefly became a giant. But the fad-and-churn critique was right about the risk that eventually undid the stock.

author: inthewoods
cardQuote: Great growth on a leaky bucket isn't good.
quote: Agree with all the commentary here but man that is some amazing growth. I haven't reviewed the S1 yet but I'd love to see their churn numbers. Great growth on a leaky bucket isn't good.
outcome: IPO'd at a $1.9B valuation in 2017; sold to Wonder for $103M in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Blue Apron went public in June 2017 and lost most of its value as churn and competition from HelloFresh and Amazon squeezed the meal-kit business. It was acquired by Wonder Group for $103 million in November 2023.
note: The comment focused on the leaky bucket rather than the growth rate; churn and customer acquisition costs were exactly what sank the public story.

author: matthew-wegner
cardQuote: They aren't taking any of these three seriously, as far as I know, so I do think pessimism is warranted.
quote:
I think it's important to place their numbers in the context of mainstream consoles. In today's living room, you have Wii (95M), Xbox 360 (67M), and PS3 (64M).

That's ~226 million consoles. The OUYA is selling well for two days, for sure, but it's a tiny fraction of the big players.

They've had 26k backers in two days. They could do 13k backers per day for an entire year and end up with ~5M consoles sold (8% of the smallest console, or 2.2% of all three). It isn't enough to get the attention of any big games. They best they'll do are Android ports.

It isn't enough to put out cheap hardware for Android. They need a seriously good storefront, a seriously good integration/account system, or a seriously good controller. They aren't taking any of these three seriously, as far as I know, so I do think pessimism is warranted.

If anything, their success at grabbing attention should put more fuel on the fire for Valve's rumored console...
outcome: Discontinued in 2015; software assets sold to Razer, storefront shut in 2019.
outcomeDetail: Ouya shipped in 2013 to weak reviews, struggled to build a game library, and sold its software assets to Razer in 2015. Razer discontinued the console that July and shut the Ouya storefront in June 2019.
note: The comment said the backer numbers were too small to attract big games and that Ouya lacked a credible storefront, account system, or controller. That is essentially what happened.

author: jdietrich
cardQuote: Add 2000w of tractive power and city traffic and you've got a recipe for disaster.
quote:
These contraptions are illegal to use in public and if they become popular the laws against them will be enforced immediately, because they're incredibly dangerous.

It is impossible to provide effective braking on a skateboard. The rider has absolutely no means of impeding their forward movement, so even if the board has effective brakes it's just going to throw them off. This is a minor problem if you're rolling around a skatepark, but it's a Big Fucking Deal if you're commuting in traffic.

It might be conceivable to overlook this failing if it weren't for the fact that tiny unsuspended wheels have almost no capacity to absorb bumps and road defects. Anyone who skated as a teenager will remember being thrown to the ground by a small piece of gravel stopping the wheel.

Add 2000w of tractive power and city traffic and you've got a recipe for disaster. Someone is going to die, their family will sue and they will quite rightly win enough money to bankrupt a small company. Boosted Boards are marketing their device as a vehicle and advertising it's suitability as a means of transport, which completely obliterates any defence they might have had. The laws against unlicensed motor vehicles will be enforced and the police will start confiscating them on sight. The electric skateboard returns to it's rightful place in the gimmick section of a sporting goods store, next to the mini-scooters and the moon shoes.

The bicycle has been a safe, practical and sustainable means of transport for over a century. Modern bicycles are lightweight, efficient and have excellent ride quality and braking. Short-range urban transport is a solved problem in all but marketing - Americans remain inexplicably certain that cycling is not for them.
storyTitle: Boosted Boards (YC S12) Unveils Its Magical Electric Skateboard
outcome: Shut down in 2020 after layoffs; assets sold off.
outcomeDetail: Boosted sold electric skateboards and scooters for years but never reached durable scale. It laid off most of its staff in March 2020 while looking for a buyer, then shut down and sold off its assets.
note: The comment predicted bankruptcy from safety liability; the actual end was a failed sale and layoffs, not a lawsuit. But the conclusion that Boosted would not survive as a small vehicle maker was right.

author: 0xbear
cardQuote: Why would anyone else buy a $700+ phone from a startup which might not even be there next year?
quote: Now we'll know exactly how many Andy Rubin fanboys there are in the world. Why would anyone else buy a $700+ phone from a startup which might not even be there next year? My prediction: a few tens of thousand units will be sold mostly in the US, darn near zero anywhere else.
outcome: Shut down in February 2020 after the Essential Phone failed to sell in volume.
outcomeDetail: Essential Phone shipped late and sold only in the US and Canada, with six-figure sales at best. The company laid off staff, canceled a second phone, and closed on February 12, 2020.
note: The comment's unit forecast was close: Essential sold in tiny volumes for a flagship phone, and the startup did not survive to support it.

author: ChuckMcM
cardQuote: I get the concept, the ultimate selfie movie, but I fear for the future of youtube's fails collection
quote: Oh goody more vaporware for HN :-(. I get the concept, the ultimate selfie movie, but I fear for the future of youtube's fails collection :-)
outcome: Shut down in January 2017; it had taken about $34M in preorders and filed for bankruptcy.
outcomeDetail: Lily collected roughly $34 million in preorders for a self-flying camera drone but repeatedly delayed shipment. It told customers in January 2017 that the camera could not be produced, then filed for bankruptcy.
note: Calling it vaporware was close to literal: Lily never shipped the drone at scale, and the preorder money became a bankruptcy claim.

author: PhantomGremlin
cardQuote: It didn't end well then, it probably won't end well now.
quote: Intel's been in the watch business before [0]. It didn't end well then, it probably won't end well now. Hey, at least they didn't spend $19 billion for a texting app.
outcome: Intel bought Basis in 2014, then discontinued the Basis Peak line in 2016.
outcomeDetail: Intel acquired Basis Science in March 2014 and marketed the Basis Peak fitness watch. Intel discontinued the product in 2016 after overheating problems and ended the brand.
note: The comment predicted Intel's watch effort would not end well; two years later Intel killed the product line.

author: PeterisP
cardQuote: I can't see how they could ever support EMV without explicit cooperation from every issuing bank
quote: "Coin does not support EMV" is an interesting statement - I can't see how they could ever support EMV without explicit cooperation from every issuing bank, which they won't have.
storyTitle: Meet Coin (YC W13), a startup creating a universal credit card
outcome: Fitbit bought Coin's payments team in 2016; the Coin card was discontinued.
outcomeDetail: Coin shipped late and never supported EMV chip cards. Fitbit acquired the company's wearable-payment platform in May 2016, and Coin's existing card was left to work only until its battery died.
note: The comment identified the fatal gap: a magstripe-only card could not survive the US shift to EMV. Coin was obsolete before it reached most customers.
